projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with August Pavis was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: 1941, I was living on 3965 Rosemont Road up in Cleveland Heights. I was born in the house there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you really?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you in '41?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, let's see,(laughing)gee-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -just tell me when you were born and I'll do the math.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: '41,'42,'43... 15. I must have been 15 cause I went in in '43 and I was 17. So I was 15 then in '41.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Still in school at that point?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Ah-

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yeah,'42 I quit like a fool, but I, you know-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: December 7th?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, not really; ah, where the heck was I? I was working - I know, I was working at my, my brother-in-law has a - had a delicatessen store up in South Yukeland. I worked for him part-time and that's when, that's when we got the news up there, but I-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -you don't remember anything specific about that day?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Not really, not really at the time, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You decided to quit school in '42, is that right?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just tired of school?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: (Chuckles.)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Or did you quit?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: I hated school. Okay, you know what I mean? I just didn't like school. I got A's in mechanical drawing and wood shop, and, and, and, things like that, but when I come to history, and English was my downfall. Math was-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -so you didn't necessarily quit to join the service, right?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: No. No, well, I really quit to join the - I liked the water. So, I quit school and I went out to-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -not the Great Lakes was it?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: No, out here, to get my passport and I - I sailed on the Great Lakes, and I sailed on the S. H. Robinson. It's an oar ship, went from here to Duluth, back and forth. I sailed on there a couple months.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: And, then I came home, and, I left home again, and went out to Cincinatti, and I worked on the Steamerama Queen that went from Cincinatti to Coney Island, New York. I sailed on there for, I was only there for about three weeks, and then I come back home. I really loved the water, that's why I joined the Navy. And I liked the, I wanted to help the war - you know what I mean.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember, before you joined the Navy, do you remember, dealing with things like rationing and that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Oh yeah,oh yeah,oh yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about that?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: We had, the, those stamps for gas, stamps for meat. Course the meat now, my brother, my younger brother, he was, he was a butcher and he worked out, he worked on Yukland, umm, I forget the name of the street down there, anyway, for Fisher Brothers - Fisher Foods, to keep us in meat on the side, you know, but things were rationed, you know, especially gas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: But we didn't use our cars that much. I had an old, at that time, my gosh, well, '41,'42, I had an old Model A-Ford. Somebody give it to me. Some old man saw me riding a little home-made motor scooter that I had, and he wanted that motor scooter and he said, I'll give you - I've got a Model A-Ford at home, but it needs a rear end. So, and I said yeah, we'll make a trade. So we traded, and we went to the junkyard, and we bought a wheel rear end with the tires and wheels and everything for $5.00 (laughing).

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Laughing.)

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: We put that thing back together.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So as far as the entire rationing, it wasn't too much of a hardship for you?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Not for me. My dad seemed to be - cope with it okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you following the war news closely at that time, before you joined up?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: I guess as much as I could have - you know-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -so when did you join the Navy?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: When; in December '43.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why in December?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, I liked the water, and I wanted to go in the Navy. I really wanted to go in the Navy. I didn't want to be drafted and go in the, go in the Marines. My two sons are Marines, but I wanted the Navy. That's why I enlisted, really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, you joined when you were 17?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: I was 17 when I went in, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have to get parental permission?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Oh, yeah, right, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Parents had no problem with it?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: No, no; no problem.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you went in what was it, late '42?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Ah, '41, I mean '43.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well at that time there wasn't much training at all. I went to Great Lakes and we were only there a couple of weeks. They were pushing for fellows to get out of there. Overseas, you know, and I wanted to go to boilermaker school. My dad was a plumber, and I wanted to, to follow more or less in his trade, you know. So, ah, but there was no openings for boilermaker school. The only thing open was - they said I could go to signal school. I said Signalman? (Laughing.) I said, I quit school; I'm a hell of a speller. That's all right, we'll send you to signal school. So, I went to this University of Chicago and, there was quite a few of us who went. University of Chicago, and we spent 3 1/2 months there. By golly, I passed with flying colors! (Laughing.) No problem! And then they sent me right over - sent me to California, and I picked up the mine sweeper, USS Weehawken. That used to be an old car ferry in New York.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: And they rebuilt the ship to ah, as a mine layer. Course we didn't take any mines over there. We were loaded with torpedos, and we took a lot of torpedos over to the different islands and so forth; dropping them off for the submarines.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you first got into the Navy, was it tough for you being thrown in with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Nah, no problem.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: No problem, no, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Got a long with people?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Lot of different guys there, I'll tell you that. (Laughing.) We had two hillbillies from the South - -never wore a pair of shoes, (laughing) oh, that was funny. Never sat on a real toilet. Gees, met a lot of different people. Lot of nice guys. Nice guys, good guys. Good guys. No problems.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you ship overseas? When did you head out to the Pacific?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, I headed out, and we picked up the ship in July 7th, sent aboard the USS Weehawken, CM-12, out of Alameda.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: On July of '44?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yeah, '44. That's when we shipped out overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your mission at that point was to deliver torpedos?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: We delivered torpedos to all these different islands and so forth, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So arrived at Tuvalu and Solomon Islands, August 31st,'44?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: September 8 arrived at Espiritu Santo and New Pepperdine Islands? (You have very good writing.)

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: A lot of islands. We went island to island.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And September 22nd it looks like you went back to Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: We went back to Pearl Harbor for a couple days.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: And we then shipped right back out again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the cargo when you shipped out again?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: We still had torpedos, more torpedos, right, right. We didn't lay any mines at all. And then later on, later on I was transferred to a mine sweeper.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: USS Facility CM-2233, and that was a sweeper. And that's where we saw a lot of action, we the sweeper. That's when we ran into a lot of Kamikazes, you know the-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -so tell me as much as you can about those days.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: The Kamikazes?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Kamikazes and the action that you saw.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, the action we saw mostly towards, uh, uh, oh man-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -that's all right.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: I just can't think anymore. Uh, on the islands towards Japan, what the hecks that-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -uh, when was this? About when was this, early '45?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: End of '44, early '45, mostly yeah. Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okinawa?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Okinawa, that's where we really ran into all the problems.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So tell me what you can about Okinawa.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, Okinawa; oh, that's when, Okinawa's when we first hit the first typhoon. Those typhoons were bad. Oh, gosh, (laughing), that scared me more than the damn air raids; those typhoons. Your ship was like a cork in the water, it just, I loved that, but I loved that. I never got sea sick in my life, and during the two typhoons I was in -- there was only, there was a few hundred fellows on the ship, it's not a big ship, but there was only five of us that never got sea sick. I was one of them; never got sea sick. We had the - I was on the bridge all the time, with the Signalman. There was always on officer on duty, or the Captain sometimes, but we always had to give them a bucket (laughing).

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: But, thank God, I never got sick. But all we ate was sandwiches, you know, they couldn't cook anything. We ate a lot of sandwiches ?"cosh coc"? (Laughing) they called that. And then -

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: -but that's where the Japanese, you'll see in that book, that's where the Japanese - they really raised hell with us. People don't realize how many ships they got. How many ships they sunk of ours, and destroyed, you know, we're in the harbor, they'd come over - at that time, if we were in harbor, different islands, and we were, we had report that the planes were coming, or we were being attacked, we'd make smoke; smoke makers. We had smoke makers on the back of our ships and everybody would make smoke so they couldn't see us, you know. But you couldn't make smoke if you were underway. But, if you were in the harbor, you know, where your ship is anchored, and so forth, they used to make smoke, and when the ship would get hit, I volunteered as one of the rescuers, and I'd go to the ship in a Captain's gig, that's the Captain's gig. There always had to be a Signalman go out anyway, and we helped put the fires out, helped take the wounded off, bring 'em back to our ship or take 'em to one of the hospital ships, if we could, and so forth. It was something. Our ship shot, I didn't myself, our ship shot three planes down, and the Japanese had a lot of mines layed around that area. My God, our ship alone, we caught 218 mines, and -

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -so how did that work? How did you sweep for mines?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, sweep for mines; I was on the lead ship. We had the big Admiral aboard our ship all the time. And the lead ship, they'd drop long cables and buoys. Buoys keep the cables up, and there's a cutter; the cable come, and there's a cutter like this-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: And as you sweep, your ship is here and the cables go this way, and you go forward and as the cable; the mines are anchored with a cable-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -right.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: And as the cable hits this, hits the mine cable, it would cut the cutter and that thing would pop up and that damn thing is, you know, they're 7-8 foot around and then we'd blow 'em up. We'd shoot at 'em with rifles and blow 'em up, and if we'd miss 'em, there's destroyers behind 'em, and they'd take care of it. But, but when we sweep -- we're the sweeper. We got --our cables are out, then there's another ship behind us and he overlaps our cable and there's so forth, and so forth; so we'd make a big pass, and those mines are poppin' up. So, our ship alone cut 218, so you can imagine how many mines they had to lay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you say you would blow them up in any way you could? Possibly shoot at them with rifles?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: We'd shoot at them with rifles.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really? Not-

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: -yeah, that's what I -- we'd do, because I wasn't working on any of the cable cutters or anything. I was the Signalman, but my job was to shoot at 'em with the rifles, and blow 'em up. I blew one up; I hit one (laughing). But we'd miss a lot of them. And then there's always destroyers behind us, and they'd, they'd really finish the mines off.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the mine sweeper was high enough in the water that it wouldn't hit these mines?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, for the first ships that went in were called the AMS That was a wooden vessel.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yeah, they were ?AMS's? And they were, they took care of magnetic mines, but they were high in the water. But we were fairly high in the water, uh --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: There was only one of our ships; just one of our ships hit a mine. And it blew them up, but none of our ships got hit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I should mention that when you were describing these cables, they were a v-shaped cable that kind of went off the back of the ship.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, yeah. The ship is here, and the cables come out and the cables always went this way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: They were on a buoy, the buoy to hold the cable up. And the cutter-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -so kind of a nice path-

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: -nice path. And the ship behind us,course they're quite a ways apart, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: The ship behind us, his cables would overlap our cable so that, so when you make a path you're makin' miles, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: It would pass, and clean these up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you do most of this around Okinawa? Is that where you were?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: A lot of the, yeah, different islands we cleaned out. And then after they dropped the bomb, that's when they were ready to invade Japan. At that time, when we were in Okinawa, and then they - course the bomb stopped that. They stopped the invasion, you know. They would have killed a lot of our men; if they would have invaded. But, after the bombs were dropped, we went into Okinawa; I mean we went into Nagasaki. We swept out Nagasaki, and Hiroshima, so our ships could get in there, we swept out -- those harbors were loaded with mines.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: They were loaded with mines, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So do you remember what you were thinking when you heard the news they dropped the bomb?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, I thought it was great myself (laughing).

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: I mean, you know, it killed a lot of their people, and we saw a lot of devastation. Boy, we went to Hiroshima and, Nagasaki, and all you could see -- you could see nothing. Everything's just wiped out, just wiped out; you could see steel, steel uh, steel structures standing a little bit. But it was devastating. But that's war, what are you gonna do?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you actually go through those cities? Tour those cities?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: We went through them, yeah. It was later on. Yeah, we went in 'em. We had to stay near the shore, you know, we couldn't go into the cities too much, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever encounter any Japanese civilians when you were in Japan?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were they like?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, they (laughing), well, I don't know if I can say this over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: The government had, you know, houses set up for the service men, you know, for girls, you know? That's the only real contact we had with them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Laughing.)

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Otherwise these guys would go crazy, these sailors, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: But they had those, whether they know it or not, they had those places set up for the service men on different islands, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: They didn't want them just foolin' around with the native women you know, that's the way it is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So this is our government, our Army.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Make sure that they had clean women.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yep. And they cleaned 'em, they made them stay clean. Yeah, yeah, yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's interesting.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yep, yep. And they'd -- but the civilians were, you know, they're - we couldn't talk to them, you know, but they'd, I don't know- they'd do anything for a cigarette.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: If you give a guy a cigarette, he'd do anything for that cigarette (laughing), gees, (laughing) oh, boy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they -- I don't know how friendly they were but, did they try to be friendly with the Americans?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: We didn't have that much contact with them, but the contact we had with a few of them, they seemed, they seemed all right, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you in Japan then?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Oh, just maybe a week off and on, you know, just uh, we very seldom got off the ship, very seldom got off the ship. Now, different islands, different islands -- if an island was halfway secure, they'd send a few of us over at a time in a Captain's gig. They'd give us three cans of beer. That's the only thing - only time we drank. Of course, I drank aboard ship. I'll tell you about that later, but they'd give us -- maybe, maybe a dozen of us would go over at a time in a Captain's gig, and you had to have a, guard with, you, with guns, you know, and we'd run around the shore and drink our three cans of beer and come back, and take turns going over. But that's the only way we could drink. But when I was on the Weehawken, we were carrying torpedos over, and they ran the torpedos with alcohol; pure alcohol. That'd come in five gallon separate cans. And I stole a five gallon can of alcohol (laughing), and I kept that on the bridge, and we'd drink that with our coffee. Oh, that stuff was good (laughing).

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Laughing.)

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: So we had our, we had our booze, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that alcohol was drinkable, huh?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Oh, yeah, oh, yeah, yep it was. Yeah, we'd drink, we'd mix it with our coffee or the orange juice, you know. We didn't have too much orange juice, but a lot of coffee, drank a lot of coffee, lot of coffee, but uh, yeah, that was drinkable, yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What else did you do for entertainment on the ship?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Nothing, we didn't do anything. The ships were small, you know, we didn't - nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Cards, or anything like that?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, we'd shoot crap, and do it once in awhile, but I, I was in two crap games and I lost everything, and I said, the hell with that, I don't play crap anymore. But, nothing, nothing, really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you ever able to go ashore for any entertainment, go see a show or-

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: -nope. Never got ashore for that, no. The only time we got ashore was just to run and drink our beer and come back, that's it, that's it. But we did come back to Pearl, what the heck we come back for? For ship repairs. We come back to Pearl, early '45 and we stayed there about four days in Pearl and got ashore there. That's the only place we really got, really got to see anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what was it like on board ship then?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, the only real exciting thing, well, was when we crossed the equator. That's when they really raised hell with us. They you know, they initiate yah. They, oh, they did all kinds of things to us. They cut our hair, they'd, they'd get a razor and just cut your hair just any old way, just rip, you know, right through it. They'd grease you up with grease, they'd hose you down, and then I remember once, we went through ah - I've got some pictures in a book I can show yah - we went through a, they had a, they had a big canvas bag. Long, it was a long bag and they'd fill that with garbage, and you'd have to crawl through that on your hands and knees and they'd beat you with these leather, leather clubs they had (laughing). And they'd beat the heck out of you while you were going through that thing. But a lot of crazy things they did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But they only did that once, right?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Just once.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The first time you crossed the equator.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Just the first time, once we crossed the equator they did that. Then we got our, oh, I forget what they call it - polliwog or whatever they call it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, from tadpole to polliwog or something like that.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yeah, something like that. I forget what the hell it was, yeah. But, but other than that, nothing. I kept busy. I was on the bridge, I was the lead Signalman for awhile.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: And I used to keep the flags sewed up. I had to sew. That was my sewing machine (laughing), I had charge of the sewing machine. And I had to, to uh, keep the flags in repair and, oh, then when we crossed the equator I made a scone Crossbone flag, I've got pictures of that I can show you, and a "go to hell" pennant. It's a long flag with white question marks, and we'd hoist that up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: That means "go to hell," it was a "go to hell" pennant.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Who were you sending that message to?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Just all the other ships; ships that were with us, yeah, they all did the same damn thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And they all knew that that's what it meant?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: They all knew that's what it meant, yeah, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Laughing.) So as Signalman you uh, that was your job, running up flags to signal other ships?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Running up flags; the light. I was good on the light, and we had the flag, we had the semifour, we had the flags that hoist on the mast and semifour, mostly the light.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm. The light was Morse code?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Oh, yeah, all Morse code, yeah, yeah. That's what we learned in school yeah, and we use a lot of that because most of the time, you couldn't use the radios, you know, radio silence and so forth. We use a lot of lights, and we'd even send messages with -- if we couldn't see another ship, we had to climb the mast and we had a big platform, there was a 24 inch searchlight up there, an arch light and you'd signal with that, up in the air, and all you'd see was a beam. You'd see the beam flashing, and you'd see another ship - you couldn't even see the ship, and he'd flash his beam up there, and you'd talk back and forth that way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: And I talked to an airplane once.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: airplane - airplanes were flying over, and they were flashing, and he sent a message; he wanted to know who we were and so forth, and-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -wow.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: It was something, it was something.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So he would flash his lights-

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: -he had a signal light. He must have had a signal light. I don't know what it was, but I saw the light blinking, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: And we talked back and forth, and the Captain was there, to make sure that he gets the message, and so forth. But other than that we didn't have any - nothing really. No shows; there was no movies aboard our ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Do you remember any other Kamikaze attacks? Anything like that?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Do I remember their attacks?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Anything specific Kamikaze attacks?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, not really. Well, let's see. The one - there was another mine sweeper with us. This was when I was on the mine layer. The other layer there was the USS Terror, CM, CM - I forget the number. But the USS Terror. She was a layer, and at that time we were making smoke. When they were comin' over, and, they, like a damn fool, started firin' anyway. And that damn Jap must've, must have turn around and saw those tracers, and he come right down and hit right in the stack of the mine layer. And we went over there, and I helped put out the fires, and helped as much as I could to get a couple fellows off of there, bring 'em back to our ship. Then they were sent to a hospital ship. One thing about the fire and rescue (laughing), one thing I liked about it (laughing), when you come back, you get two shots of whiskey (laughing).

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: You got a couple shots of whiskey to settle you down, and uh, but other than that, it's uh -

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -do you have any memories of mail call?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Nah, we didn't get-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -didn't get a lot of mail?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Nah. Not too much, really. Once in awhile you'd get mail. You know, we were out, we were out, out to sea all the time. You know, we were never in contact with too many other - let's see...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Got any close buddies on board ship?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Excuse me?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Close buddies?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Well, I had some close friends, yeah, but they, they passed away. I had a good friend that lived in Twinsburg over here ?Julia Sanny? He passed away. He was a Radioman aboard the Weehawken. He was a Radioman - good friend of mine. And Herschel Cood He lived in Oklahoma. We wrote. We wrote back and forth together, and just disappeared, you know, just lost contact with them all. I would've liked to see 'em. They had a, oh, this is about 15-20 years, 15? At least 15 years ago, they had a reunion for the Mine Layers in Texas, and I didn't go. But I probably should've went, but I never went.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You don't have any idea how many Mine Layers there were in the Pacific, do you?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Mine Layers?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: How many Mine Layers there were? I don't think -- no, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It's probably in some kind of Naval history somewhere. Did your ship -- did you lose any men on your ship?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: No, no, no. Damn near lost one. Well, (laughing) being stupidity, this guy was a muscle-man. A young fellow, he always, always showing his muscles off and so forth, always exercisin'. And we were under way, we were in convoy, and he was out, on the back of the ship, on a fantail, or a bar -- went across - I can't explain where the bar was, but he was out there chinnin' himself on this damn bar and he lost, he lost his foot, he lost, he lost his, and he went overboard. And right away I heard somebody yell, "Man overboard!" "Man overboard!" Oh, oh, the Captain had a fit. Oh, my gosh, he had a fit! So we had to turn; we had to leave the convoy, turn around, and we found him. Took a couple hours, we found him. Good thing he had -- he was smart enough to have a life jacket on him, damn fool. But that's the only man. We could've, we could've lost him. But, no, we had no problems. No damage to our ship at all. When they come over with the Kamikazes they picked out the big ships. They didn't want these little ships.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: We were on the sweeper; sweepers are small ships, you know. They wanted these big troop ships, or you know, the whatever.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How was the food on board ship? Other than the times when you had to eat sandwiches?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: The food wasn't bad. We didn't have, we didn't have the storage capacity aboard our ship, you know. Everything was powdered. You know, a lot of powdered; powdered milk, powdered eggs. When we did have a ship come and give us provisions, we'd have to -- like fruit, stuff like that, they'd leave it out, leave it out in the galley; go help yourself any time you want, cause there was no place to store it, you know, we didn't have the storage for it. And then -- I know during the, during all those air raids in Okinawa we ran out of food. And I bet we ate rice dinner, supper and breakfast for a week and a half (laughing). I'll tell yah, nothin' but rice, rice, rice. But other than that the food wasn't really that bad. You know, we ate, we had a lot, you know, during the rough weather, so forth, where they couldn't cook that much, we ate a lot of sandwiches. Course "coc" they call it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Laughing) Now, is that -- isn't that goose liver?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The, the-

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: -goose liver?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: No, just lunch meat.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, just lunch meat.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: All kinds of lunch meat.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, but that was just your colorful description of it (laughing).

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: That's the way they called it. Yeah, that was-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -I thought they used to refer to brunch, or goose liver as that.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yeah. No, that's what they called the sandwiches, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you finally come home?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: I come home, uh, when did I come home? Let's see, March 17th arrived in Balboa. Oh, 'round March, we-

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Forty -- yeah, '46; '46 we came in through, we came to Texas, Galveston. We were, I was discharged in Galveston, Texas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm. What was your reunion with your family like? When you finally got back?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Oh, it was great (laughing). It was great. I was glad to get back. I was glad to go, and glad to get back. You know, it's just, it was good to get back home. My older brother, wanted to get in the Navy so bad, but we worked for Thompson Products, and he was eight years older than I was, and he kept getin' deferred. Deferredment, deferredment, and he said, awe the hell with it, I don't want anymore deferredments. So he joined the Navy. He enlisted and he spent most his time in Okinawa. He was in the Navy, but he worked with the aircraft over in Okinawa, and Guam. And then my younger brother joined the service after I, after I did. Now, he was, he's two years younger than I was. So he didn't see any action, but he joined the Navy too. And he was on, I forget the name of the carrier. He was on a carrier and in fact I, in fact we ran across the guy, that carrier, when I was overseas, and I got permission from my Captain to go over there on a Captain's gig and see my brother. Those ships were mammoth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Oh, oh, gees (chuckles), got 5,000 men on 'em. My God, it's like a city, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Compared to our ship (laughing), our ship is, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yeah, they were mammoth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just hang around with him on the ship then?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Oh, just for a couple hours, just yeah, 'til I come back, yeah. Yeah, in fact I, another friend of mine was on a sub and we ran across them, and I got permission to go aboard the sub. They were in port, and that's a restricted, that's -- there's a lot of restrictions on those things, holy smokes. I don't know how those guys stood that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: But, but that's you know, we never, we never got to see any shows, we never USO's and so forth, we never went to USO. You know, when we did get ashore, mostly, mostly on the way back, we stopped at Pearl Harbor again. And of course, we got shore leave there, and then in Mexico. When we went through the uh, uh, uh,-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -Panama Canal?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Panama Canal. Boy, those places are wild. Wild, oh, my God, those people are wild. That's all there is is bars, and drink, and oh, my God (laughing) that's the way it is. That's the way it is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about the war, does any uh, any other particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Hmm-mmm, well, not really. Well, just mostly on Okinawa. You know we never got ashore much, like I say. But, when we first got ashore on Okinawa, that was near the, near the end of the invasion when we went ashore. There were dead Japs laying on the beach, and I picked up a rifle. In fact, I brought the rifle home. And that's you know, we really never got to see anything too much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that pretty much all the souvenir collecting you did then?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: That's all, that's all. I just got that rifle.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yeah, and I brought that home. I had to stuff my sea bag with the butt stickin' out; it got home okay, it got home okay. In fact, my son has it in Florida; it's down in Florida now. I took the mechanism out so it wouldn't shoot anyway now, but he wanted it, so when he come up to visit me, I gave it to him. But that's all, that's the only souvenir I got.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They let you carry it off the ship with it stickin' out of the bag? (Laughing.)

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Yep, stickin' out of my duffel bag (laughing), yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did a lot of guys collect things?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: I would think so, yeah. Couple, couple fellows got sabers, you know, the Japanese had big sabers; used to carry those with 'em. But other than that we were, we didn't have too much contact with-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -yeah?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: We never got into the cities and so forth, you know, course at that time, the islands were blowin' apart anyway, but gnaw, after, Okinawa was just wiped out. And my son was, my son, the Marine, he was there, course this is quite awhile and he said, "that place is beautiful. Okinawa is gorgeous," He said. (Laughing.) In fact, he and his wife went there; his wife went with him, and they lived on Okinawa, and then he, they, he was transferred to Japan, and she even went to Japan with him. And they loved it there; she loved it. (Laughing.)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. So it's a vacation spot now, Okinawa? (Laughing.) Okinawa is almost a resort?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Right! That's what he said, that's what he said. I'd like to see it. But yeah, he said it's just like a resort. Course we were there, it was just wiped out. They really, boy, they really blew that place apart. Boy, blew it apart. Blew it apart. Yeah, we'd -- especially some of these smaller islands. If we'd go ashore, if we knew there were Japs on 'em, the ships knew there were Japs on 'em, so we'd -- I didn't, but the -- they'd shoot, the only ship, we had a three-inch gun on our ship, most of them were two and fortys and single fortys for aircraft, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: And they'd shoot the island, because they knew where -- they had -- I guess they knew where the caves and so forth were, and they'd bombard the islands a little bit. Then we'd go ashore, and drink our couple cans of beer and come right back again (laughing). But that's all we - oh, let's see...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Think that covers it?

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: Pretty much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: August Pavis
sp.p: That pretty much covers it.
